challenges.title: Read It Before You Touch It
challenges.description: Your predecessor quit with zero handover. You inherit a Git repository of automation scripts and a Linux server nobody ever documented, and a dispatch release due Monday is blocked. Work out, with evidence, what is genuinely broken versus what only looks wrong. Fix the first, leave every safeguard alone, audit the server against its policy, and write down what the next engineer must never "clean up".
objectives: Before you change ANY inherited file, write MEMO.md (what each of the two disputed scripts really does, whether to fix or preserve it with evidence, and what you expect the server audit to find) and commit and push it to origin/main
Find the one genuinely broken script and fix its cause (not a workaround), then prove it with a real backup in /backups
Leave every load-bearing workaround intact - a rougher fix that keeps every safeguard beats a perfect one that removes one

Merge feature/eta-display into main cleanly (both sides' release notes kept, no conflict markers or CRLF) and push to origin without rewriting shared history; the untested WIP snapshot must never reach main
Audit the server against ~/docs/SERVER-POLICY.md and fix every finding with least privilege - never widen permissions
The instructor account must stay exactly as it is, and a leaver's home folder is evidence - keep it
Fix the network fault at its cause so that /health returns ok (HTTP 200) - do not bypass the health check or the name
Everything must survive a reboot (verification simulates one)
Commit a HANDOVER.md to main naming the load-bearing workaround and why, your branching convention, and how CALMS and DORA connect to this work
challenges.markdown:
# Read It Before You Touch It

> **Dispatch Manager:** "Our only ops person quit with zero handover. I've inherited a repo of scripts that
> route our drivers and a server nobody ever wrote anything down about. Some of it looks like junk to me, but
> I've seen someone rip out a 'junk' workaround before and it cost us three days of missed pickups - so figure
> out what's real before you change anything. We have a dispatch update going out Monday and it's blocked."

## What you are walking into

You are the new engineer at **Kente Courier Services**. You log in as `engineer` (sudo is yours, as the policy says) and land in your home directory. You inherit:

- a Git repository of the departed engineer's scripts, checked out at `~/kente-repo`
  (origin is `/srv/git/kente-app.git`; the work waiting for release lives on `feature/eta-display`),
- the application server itself, which in this exercise is **this same container**, and
- the server configuration policy: `~/docs/SERVER-POLICY.md`.

Two pieces of the automation have already caused an argument: one person is sure a script is buggy, another insists
it is intentional. Somewhere across the repo and the server something is **genuinely broken**, and something is
stopping parts of the system talking to each other. Your job is not to rewrite what you find distasteful. It is to
prove, with evidence, what is wrong versus what only looks wrong - and fix the former without touching the latter.

## Before you touch anything

Write a short `MEMO.md` and push it to `origin/main` **before your first commit that changes an inherited file**:
what you believe each disputed piece of code does, whether it is safe to change or must be preserved (with
specific evidence: a comment, a log pattern, observed behaviour - not a guess), and what you expect the server
audit to find before you run it.

## The server

Evidence is yours to gather: the logs are in `/var/log/kente-app`, the service units in `/etc/systemd/system`,
and the policy tells you the required state. Record the command and output for every finding you fix.

Things to know about this training server:

- `systemctl`, `journalctl`, `hostnamectl`, `ufw` and `reboot` are **stand-ins** (a container has no systemd and cannot
  load kernel firewall rules). They behave like the real tools and keep real state, so use them as you would on a server.
  `reboot` simulates a reboot: services come back only if they are enabled, and hostname handling follows the
  real rules.
- Docker manages `/etc/hosts` and `/etc/hostname` here. Edit them **in place** (for example with `tee` or `>`);
  `sed -i` can fail with "Device or resource busy".
- Like on a real server, `sudo` prints a warning if the machine's hostname is not in `/etc/hosts`; that is a warning, not a failure.
- Your remote refuses commits whose author email is not a company or GitHub no-reply address, and refuses
  non-fast-forward pushes. Fix problems the way you would on a shared repository.
- The scripts in `scripts/` are not marked executable in Git; the README's `sudo scripts/deploy.sh` is not
  guaranteed to work as written.

## How you are checked

Verification runs inside this container after your session and takes a few seconds. It simulates a reboot first, then checks
the repository on `origin`, every policy item, the network fix, and that every safeguard is still intact. Output
names the policy item that fails. It passes only when **everything** passes.

Not machine-graded here, but part of the real lab: the quality of your memo and handover, your two ideas for
preventing an undocumented handover, the AI-use and assumptions logs, and the live incident note.

challenges.title: Resolve the Merge Conflict
challenges.description: Merge a feature branch into main, resolve the conflict by hand, and keep everyone's work.
objectives: In /workspace/cafe, merge the student-prices branch into main
Resolve the conflict so the Coffee line shows both the new price (15) and the student price (12)
Keep every other change from both branches, leave no conflict markers, and finish the merge commit
challenges.markdown:
# Resolve the Merge Conflict

## Objective

Two people edited the same menu. Combine their work without losing either.

## Scenario

`/workspace/cafe` is a repo for a campus cafe's `menu.txt`. Two branches have diverged:

- `main` raised the coffee price and added a new item.
- `student-prices` added discounted prices.

Both changed the **same Coffee line**, so git can't decide for you.

## Task

1. Go to `/workspace/cafe` (you start there) and make sure you're on `main`.
2. Merge `student-prices` into `main`.
3. Git will stop with a conflict. Open `menu.txt` and resolve it.
   - The Coffee line must show **both** the new regular price (15) and the student price (12).
   - Every other change from both branches must be kept.
4. Finish the merge with a commit.

## Hints

- `git status` tells you which files are in conflict.
- Conflicted sections look like `<<<<<<<`, `=======`, `>>>>>>>`. Those markers must not remain in the final file.
- You can edit files with `sed`, `echo`, or `cat > file`. (There's no interactive editor in this container.)
- After editing, tell git the conflict is resolved with `git add`, then run `git commit`. The default merge message is used automatically.
- Nothing here can hurt you. If it goes wrong, `git merge --abort` puts you back at the start.

## Expected Outcome

- `main` has a merge commit joining both branches
- `menu.txt` has 6 lines, no conflict markers, and a Coffee line mentioning both prices
- `git status` is clean

challenges.title: Hello CLICE Challenge
challenges.description: Create a file called output.txt containing exactly 'Hello clice'
objectives: Create a file named `output.txt` in the `/workspace` directory
The file must contain the exact string 'Hello clice'
challenges.markdown:
# Hello CLICE Challenge

## Objective

Create a file called `output.txt` in your workspace containing exactly the string `Hello clice`.

## Task

This is the simplest possible challenge to verify your CLI environment is working.

1. Navigate to the `/workspace` directory if you're not already there.
2. Use the `echo` command to write the text `Hello clice` to a file named `output.txt`.
3. Verify the file exists and contains the correct text.

## Hints

- Use `echo` to write to a file: `echo "text" > filename`
- Check your work with `cat output.txt`
- You should see `Hello clice` printed to the terminal

## Expected Outcome

A file `/workspace/output.txt` with the exact contents:

```bash
Hello clice
```

challenges.title: Custom User Home and Shell
challenges.description: Create a user with a specific home directory, login shell, and UID.
objectives: Create user cliceuser with home /opt/cliceuser, shell /bin/bash, UID 1500
Ensure home directory exists and is owned by cliceuser:cliceuser
Verify getent passwd shows cliceuser:x:1500:1500::/opt/cliceuser:/bin/bash
challenges.markdown:
# Custom User Setup

## Objective
Create a system user with specific attributes.

## Task
Create a user named `cliceuser` with:
- Home directory: `/opt/cliceuser`
- Login shell: `/bin/bash`
- UID: `1500`
- Primary group: `cliceuser` (also GID `1500`)

The home directory must exist and be owned by this user. The account does not need a password.

## Hints
- There is a single command that can set home, shell, and UID together — check its options for creating the home directory automatically.
- After creation, you can inspect the user’s entry and the home directory’s ownership.

## Expected Outcome
`getent passwd cliceuser` shows `cliceuser:x:1500:1500::/opt/cliceuser:/bin/bash` and `/opt/cliceuser` exists with correct ownership.

challenges.title: BIND Forward Zone
challenges.description: Configure BIND to resolve a custom domain to an IP address.
objectives: Create forward zone for app.local resolving www.app.local to 192.168.1.100
Ensure named-checkconf and named-checkzone pass
Ensure dig @127.0.0.1 www.app.local returns 192.168.1.100
challenges.markdown:
# DNS Forward Zone

## Objective
Configure a local BIND resolver to answer for `app.local`.

## Task
Configure BIND to resolve `www.app.local` to `192.168.1.100`.

Your zone should include:
- A SOA record
- An NS record for `ns1.app.local`
- An A record for `ns1` (`192.168.1.10`)
- An A record for `www` (`192.168.1.100`)

Add the zone to the BIND configuration, verify the configuration and zone file are valid, start the name server, and ensure it answers queries.

## Hints
- Zone files and BIND configuration live under `/etc/bind` on Ubuntu and `/etc` / `/var/named` on openEuler — check where your system expects them.
- Two tools can validate your work before you start the server: one for the main config and one for the zone file.
- Test with a direct query to `127.0.0.1` to avoid relying on external resolvers.

## Expected Outcome
`dig @127.0.0.1 www.app.local +short` returns `192.168.1.100` and both configuration checks pass.

challenges.title: Numeric Permission 764
challenges.description: Apply exact numeric permissions to a file using chmod.
objectives: Create file /workspace/output.txt with any content
Set permissions so owner has rwx (7), group has rw- (6), others have r-- (4) — mode 764
Verify with stat -c '%a' that the mode is exactly 764
challenges.markdown:
# Numeric Permission 764

## Objective
A file at `/workspace/output.txt` must exist and have permissions `764`.

## Task
Create the file `/workspace/output.txt` (any content is fine) and configure its permissions so that:
- Owner can read, write, and execute (`rwx`)
- Group can read and write (`rw-`)
- Others can read only (`r--`)

In octal, this combination is `764`. The checker will verify the numeric mode.

## Hints
- `stat` can show the current numeric mode of a file.
- Permissions can be set using either symbolic (`u=rwx,g=rw,o=r`) or numeric (`764`) forms.

## Expected Outcome
`/workspace/output.txt` exists and its mode is `764`. Verify your work with `stat`.

challenges.title: Cron Job with Output Suppression
challenges.description: Create a recurring cron job that discards all output to prevent mail generation.
objectives: Create executable script /workspace/job.sh that appends the current date to /workspace/log.txt
Add a cron entry that runs every 5 minutes as: */5 * * * * /workspace/job.sh >/dev/null 2>&1
Verify the entry is visible via crontab -l or spool file
challenges.markdown:
# Scheduled Task with Suppressed Output

## Objective
Set up a recurring scheduled task that runs quietly.

## Task
1. Create an executable script at `/workspace/job.sh` that appends the current date/time to `/workspace/log.txt`.
2. Schedule it to run **every 5 minutes** via `cron`. The job must discard both standard output and standard error so it generates no mail.

Add the schedule without interactively editing the crontab.

## Hints
- The script needs to be executable to run from cron.
- A cron schedule has five time fields followed by a command — research the pattern for “every 5 minutes”.
- Redirecting both output streams is the key to suppressing mail.

## Expected Outcome
- `/workspace/job.sh` is executable and appends a date to the log.
- The cron table contains an entry that runs every 5 minutes and redirects output to `/dev/null`.

challenges.title: Nginx Static Site on 8080
challenges.description: Configure Nginx to serve static content on port 8080.
objectives: Create /data/www/index.html containing exactly 'hello, clice'
Configure Nginx to serve /data/www on port 8080
Ensure curl http://localhost:8080 returns hello, clice
challenges.markdown:
# Web Service on 8080

## Objective
Serve a static page on port `8080` using Nginx.

## Task
1. Create the document root and content:
   - Directory: `/data/www`
   - File: `index.html` containing exactly `hello, clice` (lowercase, with a comma and space)

2. Configure Nginx to serve `/data/www` on port `8080` and start the service. The default configuration should be adapted or supplemented so that a request to `http://localhost:8080/` returns your file.

## Hints
- On this system Nginx configuration can be added under `/etc/nginx/conf.d/` or `/etc/nginx/sites-available/`.
- After changing configuration, verify syntax and (re)start Nginx.
- `curl` can be used to test the local endpoint.

## Expected Outcome
`curl -s http://localhost:8080/` returns `hello, clice` and `/data/www/index.html` contains the same.

challenges.title: MariaDB User Grants
challenges.description: Create a database user and grant specific privileges.
objectives: Start MariaDB service
Create database appdb
Create user appuser@localhost identified by SecurePass123!
Grant SELECT and INSERT on appdb.* to that user
challenges.markdown:
# Database User Privileges

## Objective
Create a database and a restricted user with specific grants.

## Task
Using MariaDB:

1. Ensure the database server is running and create a database named `appdb` if it does not exist.
2. Create a user `appuser@localhost` identified by `SecurePass123!` if it does not exist.
3. Grant only `SELECT` and `INSERT` privileges on `appdb.*` to that user.

Do not grant additional privileges.

## Hints
- The server can be started directly without the system service manager.
- Grants can be inspected to confirm only the intended privileges were given.
- The user and database creation should be idempotent.

## Expected Outcome
- Database `appdb` exists.
- User `appuser@localhost` exists with password `SecurePass123!`.
- `SHOW GRANTS` for the user includes `SELECT` and `INSERT` on `appdb` and does not include `ALL PRIVILEGES`.

challenges.title: Failed Login Investigation
challenges.description: Analyze a web server access log to find which IP address is responsible for the most failed login attempts.
objectives: Locate all HTTP 401 (failed login) entries in /workspace/data/access.log
Determine which single IP address is responsible for the most 401 responses
Write that IP address, and only that IP address, to /workspace/output.txt
challenges.markdown:
# Failed Login Investigation

## Objective

A web server access log has been placed at `/workspace/data/access.log`.
Find the single IP address responsible for the most HTTP `401` (failed
login) responses, and write **only that IP address** to
`/workspace/output.txt`.

## Task

1. Inspect the log format — each line looks like:
   ```
   10.0.0.7 - - [10/Aug/2026:14:20:05 +0000] "POST /login HTTP/1.1" 401 128
   ```
2. Filter down to only the `401` lines.
3. Extract just the IP address (first field) from each matching line.
4. Count how often each IP appears, and find the one with the highest count.
5. Write that IP — and nothing else — to `/workspace/output.txt`.

## Hints

- `grep` can filter lines containing `401`.
- `awk '{print $1}'` pulls out the first whitespace-separated field of each line.
- `sort | uniq -c | sort -nr` is a classic combo for "count occurrences, most frequent first."
- `head -n1` gets you just the top result once sorted.
- Double-check your final file has no extra text, quotes, or trailing content —
  just the IP address itself.

## Expected Outcome

A file `/workspace/output.txt` containing exactly one IP address: the one
with the most `401` entries in the log.

challenges.title: Ghost Service
challenges.description: Stand up a small HTTP service inside this container, running as an unprivileged user, that keeps answering health checks even after your interactive session ends.
objectives: Create a non-root system user named svc-runner
Get an HTTP service listening on port 9000, running as svc-runner (not root)
The service must respond to GET /health with a JSON body containing "status":"ok" and "service":"clice"
The service must still be running and answering after you exit your shell (verification happens after your session ends, not during it)
challenges.markdown:
# Ghost Service

## Objective

Get a small HTTP service running inside this container that:

1. Runs as a **non-root** system user named `svc-runner` (not root, not
   your default user).
2. Listens on **TCP port 9000**.
3. Responds to `GET /health` with a JSON body containing
   `"status": "ok"` and `"service": "clice"` (formatting/whitespace
   doesn't matter, the fields just need to be present with those values).
4. **Keeps running after your shell session ends.** Verification happens
   once you submit, not while you're still connected — if your service
   dies the moment your interactive shell exits, it won't be running by
   the time it's checked.

There is no file to write anywhere for this one. Everything is checked
by inspecting live process, user, and network state.

## Tools available in this image

`python3`, `curl`, `netcat-openbsd`, `socat`, `sudo`, `iproute2`,
`procps` — pick whatever combination gets you there. There is more than
one valid way to build the service itself and more than one valid way
to keep it alive after your shell exits.

## Notes

- Think about what actually happens to a background process when the
  shell that launched it terminates.
- Running the service as root is the easy way and will fail the check —
  the whole point is doing it as an unprivileged user.

challenges.title: Sales Region Aggregation
challenges.description: Use awk to find the region with the highest total sales from a delimited dataset.
objectives: Read pipe-delimited /workspace/data/sales.csv (skip header)
Sum the amount column (field 3) per region (field 2)
Write only the region name with the highest total to /workspace/output.txt
challenges.markdown:
# Sales Region Aggregation

## Objective
Determine which sales region has the highest total amount.

## Task
A pipe-delimited file at `/workspace/data/sales.csv` contains sales records with the header `name|region|amount|date`.

Sum the `amount` values for each `region` (skipping the header) and write **only the name of the region with the highest total** to `/workspace/output.txt` — exactly one word, no extra formatting.

## Hints
- The file uses `|` as a delimiter — many tools can specify a custom field separator.
- You will need to accumulate a sum per region and then find the maximum.
- Look at how to skip the first line of a file.

## Expected Outcome
`/workspace/output.txt` contains a single region name that matches the highest total. No extra spaces or additional lines.

challenges.title: (Stress Test) Checker Timeout
challenges.description: Internal stress-test challenge - the checker deliberately hangs and floods stdout to verify checker_timeout is actually enforced.
objectives: Type any command and submit - the checker itself is what's being tested here
challenges.markdown:
# (Stress Test) Checker Timeout

Not a real challenge. Its checker deliberately hangs and floods stdout,
to confirm `checker_timeout` actually kills a runaway checker under real
adversarial conditions rather than just the clean cases already tested.

Do anything, submit, and confirm:

- The verdict comes back within `checker_timeout` seconds (default 20), not
  100,000 \* 0.05s later.
- The result is a clean FAIL/ENVIRONMENT ERROR, not a hang or a crash.
- `docker ps -a` shows no leftover exec processes or zombie state afterward.

Remove this challenge from the registry once you're done with it - it's
a test fixture, not real content.

challenges.title: Commit What Matters
challenges.description: Commit your new source file, and keep the noisy log file out of the repo with .gitignore.
objectives: In /workspace/project, commit the new file app.py
Make git ignore debug.log using a committed .gitignore (do not delete the file)
Finish with a clean working tree (git status shows nothing to commit)
challenges.markdown:
# Commit What Matters

## Objective

Make a proper commit: include the file that matters, and keep the noise out.

## Scenario

You've been working in `/workspace/project`. It's a git repo with one commit so far.
Since then you created two new files:

- `app.py` - your actual code. It belongs in the repo.
- `debug.log` - a throwaway log file. It does **not** belong in the repo, but you also don't want to delete it.

## Task

1. Go to `/workspace/project` (you start there).
2. Look at what git sees right now.
3. Commit `app.py`.
4. Tell git to ignore `debug.log`, and make sure that instruction is itself committed.
5. Finish with a clean working tree.

## Hints

- `git status` is your best friend. Run it often.
- `git add -A` stages *everything*, including things you may not want.
- Git reads ignore rules from a file called `.gitignore`.
- A `.gitignore` is just a file, so it needs to be committed too.

## Expected Outcome

- `app.py` is tracked and committed
- `debug.log` still exists on disk but is not tracked
- `.gitignore` is committed
- `git status` reports a clean working tree

challenges.title: Firewall Port 8080
challenges.description: Open a TCP port permanently in firewalld.
objectives: Add TCP port 8080 to the public zone permanently
Reload or ensure config is written
Verify port is listed via offline check or config file
challenges.markdown:
# Open Port 8080

## Objective
Allow TCP traffic on port `8080` in the `public` firewall zone.

## Task
Open port `8080/tcp` permanently in the `public` zone. The change should persist and be visible in the permanent configuration.

If the firewall service is not actively running, the offline configuration is sufficient.

## Hints
- `firewalld` provides both a running and an offline/permanent mode — the permanent zone files are stored under `/etc/firewalld/zones/`.
- You can query whether a port is considered open in the permanent configuration.

## Expected Outcome
Port `8080/tcp` is listed as open for the `public` zone in the permanent configuration.

challenges.title: Config Sanitization with sed
challenges.description: Edit a config file in place — remove comments and blank lines, and toggle a setting.
objectives: Remove all comment lines starting with # from /workspace/data/app.conf
Remove all empty lines from /workspace/data/app.conf
Change DEBUG_MODE=true to DEBUG_MODE=false in the same file
challenges.markdown:
# Config Sanitization

## Objective
Clean up the config file at `/workspace/data/app.conf`.

## Task
The file contains comment lines, blank lines, and a debug flag that is currently enabled.

Your goal is to leave the file in a clean state:
- No lines should start with `#`
- No empty lines should remain
- The setting `DEBUG_MODE` must be `false`, not `true`

Work directly on `/workspace/data/app.conf`. Inspect the file before and after to confirm your changes.

## Hints
- You can edit a file in place without opening an editor.
- Consider how to match lines that start with a specific character or are completely empty.
- A substitution can replace one string value with another.

## Expected Outcome
The file contains no comment or empty lines and includes `DEBUG_MODE=false`.

challenges.title: Grep Hyphen Pattern
challenges.description: Search for a string beginning with a hyphen without triggering option parsing.
objectives: Find the line containing -k in /workspace/data/options.txt
Write that line and only that line to /workspace/output.txt
challenges.markdown:
# Hyphen Pattern Search

## Objective
Extract a single line from a file that contains a hyphen-prefixed pattern.

## Task
The file `/workspace/data/options.txt` lists one option per line. One of those lines contains the string `-k` (hyphen followed by `k`).

Find that line and write **only that line** to `/workspace/output.txt`.

Be careful — some search tools interpret leading hyphens as options rather than data.

## Hints
- A naive search for `-k` may be treated as an option rather than a pattern.
- Check your tool's manual for how to mark the end of options or specify a pattern explicitly.
- The output file must contain exactly one line.

## Expected Outcome
`/workspace/output.txt` contains exactly the line from the source file that includes `-k`.
